title: Something or nothing at the start
hookLine: a sleepover question: before everything, something or nothing?
carry: Being came first, and wished to be many
tomorrow: a bird tied to a string flies off every way. where does it land?

cards: Lights out at a sleepover, and somebody asks the question that ends all sleep. Before anything existed, was there something, or nothing? One voice says nothing.
Another says you can't get something from nothing. Inside the Chandogya Upanishad, the same argument is already running, and Uddalaka pauses his son's lesson to take it on.

teach.h: BEING ALONE, ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.
teach.b: In the beginning, my dear, the father says, this was Being alone. One only, without a second. The word is sat: being, what is.
Then he names the other view, fairly.
Some say that in the beginning there was only non-being, and from non-being, being was born. That view has its own home in the tradition.
Another Upanishad, the Taittiriya, says it in its own voice: in the beginning this was non-being, and from it being was born. Its best case goes like this.
Before names and forms, there was no thing at all to point to, no this, no that; everything nameable came later. Uddalaka answers with a question. How could being come out of non-being?
So, he says: in the beginning, Being alone, one without a second. And his Being doesn't sit still.
It thought: may I be many, may I grow forth. It sent forth heat.
Heat sent forth water, which is why, he says, a person who grieves or sweats grows wet. Water sent forth food, which is why rain brings a harvest.
Named plainly, that is the Upanishad's picture of creation: not a maker building from outside, but the one Being becoming many from within. Vedanta calls that Being Brahman.

Some commentators read the Taittiriya's non-being as the not-yet-named, so the two lines can meet. Either way, the tradition kept both texts. And when the great saying comes, the that in that you are will point back here.

how: Vedanta teachers read Chandogya 6.2 alongside the Taittiriya's line on non-being, and commentators explain how the two fit; in study, both passages are heard as scripture.

o: that you are: that, the Being under everything
that one over there is you, a lookalike
you are not yet that, but you will be

games.q: two views of the beginning. tap the pairs.

s: Hindu scriptures all give the same account of how everything began
the Chandogya says Being came first; the Taittiriya says non-being, then being. the tradition kept both.
Uddalaka links tears and sweat to heat
heat sent forth water, so when a person grieves or sweats, water comes from heat, he says.

games.q: at a debate club, you're told to argue the side you don't hold: in the beginning there was non-being. what's its best case?
o: before names and forms, there was no thing at all to point to.
no Hindu text ever says it, so there's no case to make.
it means the world is fake and nothing in it matters.
games.why: the Taittiriya says it in its own voice: non-being first, then being. some commentators read non-being as the not-yet-named. Uddalaka answers it with a question.

practice: If there's paper near you, write two short lines by hand. In the beginning, being. In the beginning, non-being.
Read each one slowly, as if it were your own view, and breathe between them without choosing.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi: that you are. In the Chandogya, the that is Being, one without a second, whose first wish was to be many.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one only, without a second. The father's words for Being in the beginning.

carryVoice: For the road: Being came first, and wished to be many. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1–4 (in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second; some say non-being, and being born from it; how could being be born from non-being?; Being thought, may I be many, may I grow forth, and sent forth heat; heat sent forth water, so when one grieves or sweats water comes from heat; water sent forth food, so wherever it rains food is plentiful)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1 (in the beginning this was non-being; from it being was born)
